overshadow

/oh-ver-SHAD-oh/ - the stress falls on SHAD · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Overshadow means to make something seem less important or noticeable by comparison.

Both paintings hang in the same room, but the famous one overshadows its quieter neighbor, and most visitors never notice the better picture.

Example

The museum unveiled both finds the same morning — a complete dinosaur skeleton and a modest fossil fern. The skeleton overshadowed the fern completely: crowds three deep at one case, an empty bench at the other, though the fern was the older and rarer find.

Overshadow is more precise than 'beat' or 'outdo' because nothing is taken from the lesser thing — the fern lost none of its value. It is attention that shifts: standing in something bigger's shadow, the quieter achievement simply looks smaller than it is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

upstage: To upstage someone is to steal the audience's attention in the middle of their moment, often deliberately — the theater's word for scene-stealing. Overshadow needs no intent and no shared stage: one thing simply stands near something bigger and gets noticed less. Upstage is an act; overshadow is a condition.

dwarf: To dwarf something is to make it look small by sheer physical size — the new tower dwarfs the chapel whether anyone is looking or not. Overshadow works on attention rather than measurement: the smaller thing keeps its size and its worth but loses its audience.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

highlight: to pull something forward into everyone's notice

spotlight: to aim the audience's attention straight at it

Where it sits · how completely the rival disappears from view — outshine → overshadow → eclipse

outshine vs. overshadow: To outshine a rival is simply to do better; overshadow goes further, dimming how the rival's work is seen, however good it remains.

eclipse vs. overshadow: Eclipse pushes past overshadow: an overshadowed book still finds readers in the bestseller's shadow, but an eclipsed one drops out of print — blotted from view as the moon blots out the sun.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — over-

Prefix — over-: above, beyond

Root — shadow

Root — shadow: the dark shape cast where light is blocked

Put it together

Put it together: Over- (above) + shadow (the dark cast shape) = to throw one's shadow down over something from above. Old English used it of clouds and towers; the modern sense keeps the picture — whatever stands in a taller thing's shadow is still there, just harder to see.

Use the root in a new word: shade

Use the root in a new word: shade: They ate lunch in the shade of the oak — shade and shadow both grew from the same Old English sceadu, one dark shape with two spellings.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Overshadow is the word when one thing makes another look smaller merely by standing beside it — no malice required and no contest held. If the rival is actively beaten, outshine says so; if attention is stolen mid-performance, upstage; and when the lesser thing vanishes from view altogether, eclipse marks the far end of the same scale.
